cards.definition: Direct communication between paid representatives and prospects that leads to transactions, customer satisfaction, account development, and profitable relationships.
The planning, organizing, leading, and controlling of personal contact programs designed to achieve the sales and profit objectives of the firm.
The person responsible for managing the field sales operation, either as a first-line manager or higher in the hierarchy.
The spread of markets and competition across national borders, forcing sales forces to shift from a local to a global focus.
Faster technology transfer that narrows the window of product differentiation and raises the value of selling and relationship skills.
The explosion of new products, brands, channels, and price points that sharply increases knowledge demands on salespeople.
Selling built on selling skills, product/price/service, differentiation through products, and a short-term sales revenue focus.
Selling that creates customer value by addressing important customer problems through a supplier-customer relationship more intimate than transactional selling.
Multiple seller contacts matched to multiple buyer contacts, replacing the traditional single-point "lone wolf" buyer-seller interface.
The internal and external web of contacts a salesperson needs to prospect, close complex deals, and deliver customer solutions.
Profit-based performance measures (time to close, gross margin, discounting, promotional and post-sale support) that replace pure sales volume.
The sequence guiding sales programs — seeing the big picture, defining sales force roles, structuring the sales force, building competencies, and leading the sales force.
Sets of knowledge, skills, behaviors, and attitudes needed to be effective as a sales manager across industries and organizations.
Understanding the industry, understanding the organization, and taking actions consistent with company goals and strategy.
A sequence of conversations and activities giving ongoing feedback and encouragement, achieved through verbal feedback, role modeling, and building trust.
Designing teams properly, creating a supportive environment, and managing team dynamics.
Integrity and ethical conduct, managing personal drive, and self-awareness and development.
Cultural knowledge and sensitivity plus the ability to design and run a global selling program.
Understanding the productivity potential of new technology and implementing sales force automation and CRM.
Integration of communications and computer technology into selling tasks to increase sales force efficiency and effectiveness.
Defining the business mission, developing specific measurable goals, and designing a strategy for achieving them.
Statement of the customers a firm wishes to serve, the needs to be fulfilled, and the activities and technologies used to fulfill them.
The cascading of corporate goals down through business unit, marketing, sales department, district, salesperson, and major account objectives.
Porter's three positions for creating superior customer value — low cost, differentiation, and niche.
Vigorous pursuit of cost reductions from experience and tight cost control.
Creating an offering perceived as unique, leading to high brand loyalty and low price sensitivity.
Servicing one target market very well and dominating sales within that segment.
The set of integrated decisions and actions a business takes to achieve its marketing objectives by addressing customers' value requirements.
Aggregating customers into groups that share characteristics, have similar needs, and respond similarly to a marketing program.
The selection and prioritizing of the segments a company will serve.
Decisions about product, price, distribution, and promotion that shape how consumers perceive the product, brand, and company versus competitors.
The Level 2 processes organizations develop to create customer value — go-to-market strategy, PDM, SCM, and CRM.
The decisions defining who will perform the essential selling activities and for which customers.
All activities needed to serve a customer properly, grouped as interest creation, prepurchase, purchase, and postpurchase.
Outside businesses (manufacturers' reps or brokers) given exclusive contracts to sell within specified geographic areas; not employees.
Customer contact that uses telecommunications technology for personal selling without direct, face-to-face contact.
The process of developing, producing, and launching new offerings, with the sales force a key source of new product information.
The integration and organization of information and logistics activities across firms to create and deliver goods and services that provide value to customers.
A comprehensive set of processes and technologies for managing relationships with current and potential customers across marketing, sales, and service.
A tool for planning how the sales force will perform its role in achieving the firm's objectives; the Level 3 decisions.

cards.term: Elements of the sales force program
cards.definition: Sales potential and forecast, account relationship strategy, desired selling actions and behaviors, sales force size and budget, organizational structure, competency development, and leadership system.
The type or types of relationship a firm intends to develop with its customers, including plans for acquiring, maintaining, and developing them.
A relationship based on a product of acceptable quality, competitively priced, and a process convenient for the buyer.
A relationship based on the customer's demand and willingness to pay for a sales effort that creates new value beyond the product itself.
A relationship whose primary function is to leverage all corporate assets of the supplier to contribute to the customer's strategic success.
An estimate of maximum industry demand in a time period based on the number of potential users and their purchase rate.
The maximum amount a firm can sell in a time period under optimum conditions; the company's share of market potential.
Predicting future levels of demand, which is essential for budgeting, quotas, territories, and planning.
A multifactor index combining population, income, and retail sales into a composite indicator of consumer demand by geographic area.
A forecast built by aggregating salespeople's own volume projections for customers in their territories.
A forecast produced by soliciting and pooling the judgment of a group of experienced managers.
Economic series that change in advance of company sales and can therefore be used to predict sales and turning points.
Actual sales divided by the appropriate seasonal index so that seasonal effects are removed before forecasting.
The simplest time-series technique, assuming the best estimate for the next period is the current level of sales.
The average absolute percentage error across periods, used to compare forecasting accuracy across methods and products.
A forecast equal to the average revenue achieved over the several most recent periods.
A forecast that emphasizes recent information and systematically discounts older information.
The alpha weight (between 0 and 1) in exponential smoothing; low values give stability, high values respond faster to change.
Fitting a straight line by least squares to express the relationship between sales and time.
A sudden change in a trend, which quantitative forecasting methods predict poorly.
The phenomenon in which a portion of current sales is a function of customer relationships built by selling effort in prior years.
Sizing the sales force from the number of accounts, call frequency, and call length required, divided by the selling time available per salesperson.
Sizing the sales force by estimating how sales respond to different levels of selling effort, then evaluating sales and profit impact.
Setting sales force size and budget by multiplying the sales forecast by a predetermined percentage of sales.
A set of planned selling expenses prepared on an annual basis to reach the sales manager's objectives.
A four-quadrant budgeting tool identifying revenue sources — account management, leverage selling, convergence selling, and new business development.
Allocating selling effort across generating new accounts, managing existing accounts, balancing sales versus profits, and personal time management.
Spending selling time with prospects who are likely to become good customers, in order to acquire new accounts.
A profile of what the best prospect looks like, used to decide which leads are worth pursuing.
Cold canvassing, direct mail, trade shows, directories, the Internet and Webcasting, and referrals.
Determining whether a prospect is likely to convert into a buying customer.
The prospect must have a need, buying authority, and the ability to pay.
Total direct selling expenses for a period divided by the total number of sales calls made in that period.
Costs attributable to an individual salesperson — compensation, travel, lodging, entertainment, and communications.
The sales volume necessary to cover the direct selling expenses of calling on an account.
The smallest customer worth pursuing, found by dividing the cost of selling by the gross margin percentage.
Prioritizing accounts on one characteristic, usually total sales volume, as in ABC account classification.
Classifying accounts on two dimensions — account opportunity and competitive position — to allocate selling effort across four quadrants.
The magnitude of an account's present and future need for the salesperson's offering.
The strength of the salesperson's present and future relationship with an account.
Core accounts, growth accounts, drag accounts, and problem accounts, each warranting a different level of selling investment.
A call allocation model that assigns calls based on the sales response of each account over a period of time.
The estimated relationship between the number of sales calls made over a period and the sales generated for a particular account.
A model that prioritizes opportunities by their stage in the selling process and their probability of resulting in a sale.
Possible needs that have not been verified with key people in the account.
Opportunities with a verified need, confirmed intention to buy, approved funding, and an identified time frame.
Opportunities where all buyers have been contacted, needs developed, and the sale is at least 50 percent through the selling cycle.
The image ranking opportunities from unqualified at the top, through qualified, to the best few at the bottom of the funnel.
Close the best few first, prospect for unqualified opportunities second, and work qualified opportunities last to keep the funnel full.
The sum of a customer's discounted flow of future profit contributions, used as a forward-looking resource allocation metric.
Planning and controlling the use of selling time to increase the share spent face to face with customers.
The four typical stages business buyers move through — recognition of needs, evaluation of options, purchase decision, and implementation and evaluation.
A purchasing situation in which the product has been bought before and no change is desired; it simply replenishes inventory.
A purchasing situation in which some changes are anticipated, so the evaluation of options becomes much more extensive.
The most complex purchasing situation, in which the seller can add value during recognition of needs, evaluation of options, and implementation.
The dynamic in which demand for a business product is derived from demand for the customer's own products and services.
A written offer by a seller to provide a product or service to a purchasing organization.
A notice a customer sends to qualified suppliers asking them to bid on a project with a certain set of specifications.
Linked trading-partner computer networks that create a secure private environment for real-time order, inventory, and shipping information.
A detailed analysis of a product focusing on the relative cost of providing a necessary function or service at the desired time and place with the necessary quality.
Evaluation of a supplier on delivery reliability, price, service, and technical competence.
Segmentation of a customer's supplier base into levels — in-supplier, preferred, extended, and partner — reflecting the importance of the relationship.
Situations in which several people in the customer's organization must give approval before the sale can take place.
All the people formally or informally involved in a purchasing decision — anyone who must say yes, or who can influence those who do.
The set of issues or concerns a buying center member considers when deciding whether to approve or recommend a purchase or supplier.
The person or committee with power to give final approval to buy; focused on performance and return for the money spent, and can say yes when everyone else says no.
The buying center member who judges the impact of the purchase on the job that they or their people perform; implementation-oriented and tactical.
The gatekeeper who screens out products and suppliers that fail to meet specifications; can say no but cannot say yes.
The insider who helps guide the salesperson to the right people and information so that the sale can be successfully concluded.
The five general stages a buyer-seller relationship passes through — awareness, exploration, expansion, commitment, and dissolution.
The factors that drive parties toward a fully committed relationship — creating value, meeting expectations, and building trust.
The perception that the rewards exceed the costs associated with establishing or expanding a relationship.
The rules or norms parties develop with respect to acceptable conduct and performance in a relationship.
The opinion that an individual's word or promise can be believed and that the customer's long-term interests will be served.
Honesty, competence, dependability, customer orientation, and likability.
The market, financial, organizational, operational, personnel, and competitive information a seller gathers about an account.
Preinteraction (planning skills), interaction (relating, discovery, advocating, closing), and postinteraction (supporting skills).
A selling model using a constructed series of statements about an offering designed to stimulate a positive response from the customer.
A highly structured standard presentation given to each customer, requiring little preparation once mastered.
A selling model oriented toward discovering and meeting customers' needs, with the salesperson testing assumptions about the customer's problems.
A selling model based on a formal study of the customer's operations, followed by a written proposal and formal presentation.
The phase in which the salesperson collects thoughts and organizes interaction strategy prior to meeting the customer face to face.
The preinteraction planning that differentiates top performers from average salespeople.
Setting objectives, knowledge management, information gathering, and rehearsal before a sales call.
What takes place during the face-to-face encounter with a customer, including gaining access, relating, discovery, advocating, and closing.
Securing face time with decision makers through direct personal contact, phoning ahead, personal letters, e-mail, or referrals.
A salesperson's fear of making contact with a customer.
The tension a buyer feels on meeting a salesperson, arising because people don't like to be sold; they like to buy.
The ability to put the other person at ease in a potentially tense situation.
Propriety, competence, commonality, and intent.
Understanding what is on the prospect's mind rather than focusing the discussion on the product and its benefits.
The logical, practical, or functional reasons for buying, usually involving money or productivity.
The individual reasons behind a purchase decision — respect, approval, power, and recognition.
Questions answerable with a simple yes or no or by selecting from a list; used to gain feedback and commitment.
Questions that cannot be answered yes or no, used to identify and explore a topic.
Closed-ended questions asking the other person's permission to ask questions or probe further into a subject.
Questions focusing on factual information about the business, the person, or the current situation.
Open-ended questions that uncover feelings about a situation and its potential consequences.
Questions that check one's understanding and get agreement concerning a statement.
The ability to clearly and fully present a solution that customers can see will help address their needs.
Confirming with customers that the goods and services being offered match their requirements and satisfy their needs.
The tangible or intangible characteristics of a product or service.
Statements of how a product or service can help a customer satisfy an explicit or stated need.
Test results, testimonials, demonstrations, or trial periods offered to support a benefit claim.
Wilson Learning's method for handling customer concerns — Listen, Share, Clarify, Problem-solve, and Ask for action.
Asking the customer for a commitment, either for an order or to advance the purchasing process.
An opinion-seeking question used as an indicator of how close the client is to making a purchase decision.
A close posing a series of questions designed to narrow the prospect's choice and help make a final selection.
A close that summarizes the benefits accepted during the call, combined with an action plan requiring the customer's commitment.
The phase following the transaction, involving supporting skills that service the sale and build the relationship.
All the efforts involved in servicing the sale and building a lasting, growing relationship after the purchase.
Supporting the buying decision, managing the implementation, dealing with dissatisfaction, and enhancing the relationship.
Selling additional products and services to an existing account.
Selling bigger or enhanced products or services to an account, typically producing higher margins and greater dollar commitments.
Systematically recording what was learned about the prospect and customer after each interaction so it can be used in the future.
